## Where the ground moved

The feed covers {{< marimo value="seismic_analysis.weekly.days" >}} days,
from {{< marimo value="seismic_analysis.weekly.period_start" >}} to
{{< marimo value="seismic_analysis.weekly.period_end" >}}. Most epicenters
trace the boundaries of tectonic plates: the Pacific Ring of Fire, the
Alpine–Himalayan belt, and the mid-ocean ridges. @fig-map places every event,
sized by magnitude.

::: {#fig-map .column-page}
```{=html}
<div class="chart chart-map" id="map-chart" role="img" aria-label="World map of the week's epicenters"></div>
```

Epicenters of the week's events. Circle area follows magnitude, and events of
magnitude 6 or larger are outlined in dark red.
:::

::: {.column-margin}
**Reading the map.** Each circle is one epicenter, the point on the surface
above where a rupture began. Hover a circle for its place, magnitude, and USGS
review status.
:::

## Activity through the week

A single large earthquake brings aftershocks, so a busy day often follows a
strong event.

::: {#fig-days}
```{=html}
<div class="chart chart-days" id="days-chart" role="img" aria-label="Events per day with the largest magnitude of each day"></div>
```

Events per day. The label above each bar is that day's largest magnitude.
:::

## Felt reports

USGS collects "Did You Feel It?" reports from the public. A count measures how
many people reported shaking, which depends on population near the epicenter
as much as on the earthquake itself.
:::

## Magnitude is logarithmic

Earthquake magnitude is a logarithmic measure of recorded ground-motion
amplitude. One magnitude unit corresponds to about ten times the amplitude and
roughly 32 times the released energy [@gutenberg1956]. Choose a comparison
magnitude for the week's largest event.

{{< marimo cell="magnitude_reference_control" >}}

{{< marimo cell="magnitude_comparison" >}}

## Frequency and magnitude

Small earthquakes vastly outnumber large ones. The Gutenberg–Richter relation
describes the cumulative count of events at or above magnitude $m$ as a line
on a logarithmic scale [@gutenberg1944]. @fig-gutenberg compares the observed
counts with a straight-line fit. A global feed records small events unevenly,
so the observed curve flattens at its low end.

::: {#fig-gutenberg}
```{=html}
<div class="chart chart-gutenberg" id="gutenberg-chart" role="img" aria-label="Cumulative event counts by magnitude with the fitted Gutenberg–Richter line"></div>
```

Cumulative events at or above each magnitude, on a logarithmic count scale.
Points are observed. The line is the descriptive fit, drawn across its range.
:::

{{< marimo cell="frequency_magnitude_relation" >}}

{{< marimo cell="frequency_threshold_control" >}}

{{< marimo cell="frequency_threshold_summary" >}}

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
## One week is a snapshot

The fit summarizes a single global week. Treat the b-value as a description
of this record rather than an estimate of regional hazard, which needs long
catalogs for one region.
:::

## About the data

The week holds {{< marimo value="seismic_analysis.weekly.source_events" >}}
events, {{< marimo value="seismic_analysis.weekly.qualified_events" >}} of them
at or above magnitude
{{< marimo value="seismic_analysis.weekly.catalog_minimum_magnitude" >}}.
Every record keeps its time, epicenter coordinates, review status, and USGS
event page. The record is the USGS GeoJSON summary feed of magnitude 2.5 and
larger earthquakes for 22 to 29 January 2024 [@usgsfeed].
